description: ORBITA AI is a solo student project focused on creating an interactive educational space game. I am building a web-based lunar outpost simulator where young players make engineering decisions and balance critical resources such as power, life support, food production, and radiation protection. The goal is to make space engineering engaging, understandable, and fun for young learners.
summary:
ORBITA AI is an educational browser game that puts young learners in command of a lunar outpost. Players design a base using eight modules, then manage power, oxygen, water, food and crew well-being across five progressive missions.

Engineering choices have visible consequences: greenhouse production consumes water, research competes with life support for power, and shelter placement affects crew safety during solar particle events. Emergencies require players to weigh immediate costs against future risks. Engineering reports and mission debriefs explain why their decisions worked or failed.

The game combines illustrated lunar environments, interactive construction, achievements and saved progress to make engineering trade-offs tangible and engaging. It runs in a browser without registration. All resource rates and scenarios are clearly labeled as simplified teaching assumptions; no live NASA data or external AI model is integrated.
details:
ORBITA AI is an educational browser strategy game where players design and operate a lunar outpost for four astronauts.

Players place eight modules: Habitat, Life Support, Solar Array, Battery Storage, Greenhouse, Storm Shelter, Research Lab and Water Processing. Terrain and placement affect modeled solar generation, water extraction, utility connections and shelter access. An engineering report updates as the layout changes.

Five progressive missions introduce resource management and emergencies. Food production consumes water, research competes with life support for power, and batteries support operations during scheduled shadows. Solar particle events require players to choose between shelter access, protected transfer and continued surface work. Debriefs explain the consequences and encourage players to revise their designs.

The intended benefit is to make engineering trade-offs understandable through experimentation. Learning outcomes have not yet been evaluated in a classroom.

The game uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and SVG artwork, with local saved progress and GitHub Pages hosting. ChatGPT/Codex assisted coding, debugging, text drafting and generation of vector artwork. Visible labels identify SI-generated artwork.

NASA educational resources support the Science Notebook and contextual debriefs about life support and radiation shielding. All numerical rates, terrain and health penalties remain simplified teaching assumptions. No live NASA feed, calibrated NASA dataset or external AI service is integrated.
